title: Louis Bachelier's Theorie de la speculation: Circulation and Reception
abstract: Louis Bachelier's Theorie de la speculation (1900) introduced a probabilistic model of Brownian motion in a study of financial fluctuations, five years before Einstein's physical theory. By connecting probability distributions with the heat equation and studying speculation and option valuation, Bachelier anticipated central developments in probability, physics, and mathematical finance. How widely did the thesis circulate before its broader significance was recognized? Drawing on library correspondence, surviving copies, accession registers, provenance marks, historical catalogues, and acquisition lists, this article reconstructs its international circulation and reception in two forms: the separate Gauthier-Villars dissertation and its publication in the Annales scientifiques de l'Ecole normale superieure. It identifies thirty-eight foreign academic institutions in the official dissertation exchange network for 1900 and documents its operation. University exchanges, commercial purchases, journal distribution, and personal presentations provided complementary channels. American holdings reveal its geographical reach, including receipt at Cornell in April 1900. Contemporary reviews and subsequent uses establish selective engagement in mathematics, actuarial science, and economics, including transmission without attribution. An examination of probability composition and diffusion clarifies the thesis's place in the history of stochastic processes and its relationship to physical Brownian motion. Columbia's journal volume, accessioned in 1901 and borrowed by Mandelbrot in 1961, connects early dissemination with renewed interest. Distinguishing availability from documented reading and use, the study shows that delayed recognition coexisted with early international circulation and a dispersed readership across scientific traditions.
